result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.global_efficiency()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate the global efficiency of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L24597-L24663){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.global_efficiency() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Efficiency](/assets/graphs/algo-efficiency.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A seven-edge graph with source s on the left and target t on the right, both drawn in the accent color. A three-hop shortest path from s to t through the upper row is highlighted in accent. A small heads-up display in the top right reports the pair distance d(s,t) = 3, the pair efficiency E(s,t) = 1/3 (its reciprocal), and the graph's global efficiency E_glob = 5/12, averaged over every pair." width="100%"} Global efficiency is the average efficiency over all pairs of nodes, where efficiency is the multiplicative inverse of the shortest path distance. It measures how efficiently information flows through the network. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The global efficiency (between `0` and `1`). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Latora and Marchiori (2001) introduced global efficiency as an information-flow measure on a comparable $[0, 1]$ scale across any topology: $E_{\mathrm{glob}}(G) = \dfrac{1}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i \ne j} \dfrac{1}{d(i, j)}$, with the convention that $1/d(i, j) = 0$ whenever $j$ is unreachable from $i$. A complete graph achieves the maximum of $1$; an empty graph or one made of isolated vertices reaches $0$. Unlike the closely related mean distance, global efficiency behaves gracefully on disconnected inputs because unreachable pairs contribute exactly $0$ rather than diverging. The computation reuses the all-pairs unweighted BFS pass, so cost is $O(V(V + E))$ time and $O(V^2)$ space. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A complete graph has every pair of nodes directly connected, so its global efficiency is at its maximum of 1: ::: {#652eaf11 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() n = 5 for i in range(n): graph.add_node(label=f"n{i}") nodes = sorted(graph.get_node_ids()) for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 1, n): graph.add_edge(nodes[i], nodes[j]) # Returns close to 1.0 graph.global_efficiency() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1.0 ``` ::: ::: Sparser topologies have longer average shortest paths and therefore lower efficiency; a star graph is much more efficient than a path of the same size, since every node is at most 2 hops from any other through the hub: ::: {#1b1ca0ad .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} path = ec.Graph() path.add_path_graph(10) star = ec.Graph() star.add_star_graph(10) # Path efficiency is much lower than star efficiency (path.global_efficiency(), star.global_efficiency()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (0.4286596119929453, 0.6) ``` ::: :::
